metadata.title: Animate Telomere Crisis with Claude Code

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — open on the Claude UI, ask shown answered
beats.narration_text: Konnichiwa, Liam. One Claude prompt. An animated telomere crisis — four erosion stages, a fork, and the one-in-a-million survivor.

props.command: claude "Port the telomere-crisis plate from plates_gen.py p02() into Manim. 4 X-chromosome glyphs, caps shrinking left to right. Fork at end: upper=survivor, lower=dead end with VERM X-mark."

beats.role_note: The mechanism before the build — what erosion IS
beats.narration_text: Telomeres are the repetitive caps on chromosome ends. Every cell division erodes them a little. This plate shows four stages of that erosion — each chromosome pair has caps that get shorter stage by stage until almost nothing is left.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — four chromosome X-glyphs with shrinking caps, left to right; label 'erosion stage 1→4'; caps go from large GREEN dots to tiny VERM dots

beats.role_note: Stakes before the build — the bottleneck and the survivor
beats.narration_text: At crisis, most cells die — the vast majority dead end. But rarely, one cell reactivates telomerase, survives with a scrambled genome, and that survivor is a cancer cell. We're animating that one-in-a-million bottleneck.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — fork diagram: upper branch 'survivor (telomerase ON, genome scrambled)'; lower branch 'dead end (majority)'; VERM X-mark on lower; stat card 'most cells die at crisis'

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — the ACTUAL B05_TelomereCrisis class, trimmed to what teaches
beats.narration_text: Read it. The chromosome glyph is two diagonal lines plus four cap dots — that is the entire shape record. The cap radii are a list: sixteen, eleven, six, two. One list comprehension builds all four glyphs in a LaggedStart. The fork is two lines drawn from a branch point — one up to the survivor, one down to the dead end. The X-mark is two crossing Lines in VERM. The Flash is the punctuation — it tells the eye where the bottleneck lives.

props.title: scenes.py — B05_TelomereCrisis
props.code:
# scenes.py — Claude Code output
SKY="#56B4E9"; BLUE="#0072B2"; GREEN="#009E73"
VERM="#D55E00"; GRAY="#7c7c7c"
CAP_R=[0.32,0.22,0.12,0.04]  # shrinking caps

class B05_TelomereCrisis(Scene):
  def construct(self):
    glyphs=VGroup()
    for i,cr in enumerate(CAP_R):
      x=-5.0+i*2.5; arm=0.7
      cap_col=GREEN if i<3 else VERM
      g=VGroup(
        Line([x-arm,arm,0],[x+arm,-arm,0],
             color=BLUE,stroke_width=4),
        Line([x-arm,-arm,0],[x+arm,arm,0],
             color=BLUE,stroke_width=4),
        *[Dot([x+dx*arm,dy*arm,0],radius=cr,
              color=cap_col,fill_opacity=0.9)
          for dx,dy in [(-1,-1),(1,-1),(-1,1),(1,1)]]
      ); glyphs.add(g)
    self.play(LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(g) for g in glyphs],
              lag_ratio=0.22,run_time=1.8))
    bp=np.array([1.8,0,0])
    fk=VGroup(
      Line(bp,bp+[1.5,1.2,0],color=GRAY,stroke_width=3),
      Line(bp,bp+[1.5,-1.2,0],color=GRAY,stroke_width=3))
    self.play(GrowFromPoint(fk,bp),run_time=0.7)
    xmark=VGroup(
      Line([3.1,1.0,0],[3.4,1.4,0],color=VERM,stroke_width=6),
      Line([3.1,1.4,0],[3.4,1.0,0],color=VERM,stroke_width=6))
    self.play(FadeIn(xmark),run_time=0.4)
    self.play(Flash(xmark.get_center(),color=VERM,
              line_length=0.25,num_lines=12,flash_radius=0.5))
    self.wait(0.8)

beats.role_note: Manim render of B05_TelomereCrisis — watch LaggedStart reveal and fork flash
beats.narration_text: Run it. Watch left to right — each chromosome glyph fades in, caps visibly smaller on each successive glyph. Green at the start, tipping to vermillion on that last, almost-bare chromosome. Then the fork splits: survivor branch up, dead-end branch down. The X-mark appears. The Flash fires. That flash is where the biology happens — one cell in ten thousand makes the survivor branch.

The change. Revise: make caps progressively shrink with dot animate dot scale as each chromosome appears, so the erosion is motion not just size. Add a Circle glow on the survivor's caps and pulse the dead-end X-mark so the viewer feels the asymmetry — one branch is alive, one is not.

beats.act: OUTPUT — revised animation with erosion motion
beats.role_note: Manim render of B07_TelomereCrisisFlow — caps shrink in motion, survivor glow, X-pulse
beats.narration_text: Watch the revision. Each glyph appears with full-size caps, then the caps shrink — the erosion is a movement, not just a state. The fork appears. Survivor caps glow green. The dead-end X pulses in vermillion. Two branches, two outcomes, and the asymmetry is obvious: one branch has life in it, the other is a flat line.

The motion taught: it is a numbers game. The erosion is relentless, the fork inevitable, and the surviving lineage is the one that cheated the clock. Claude ported four glyph stages, a fork split, and a flash in one prompt. The revision added motion to the erosion — caps that literally shrink, so the viewer sees the biology happen, not just the result.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — summary card: 'erosion is a process, not a state'; four-stage sequence recap; 'the survivor is the exception' highlighted in GREEN

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read aloud AND discussed. greeting = 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt into Claude: add a fifth glyph at the far right of the erosion sequence — fully bare, no caps at all — and label the moment 'crisis.' Then animate a probability weight on the fork: the dead-end branch is thick, the survivor branch is thin. Why run it? Because the visual weight encodes the actual odds. Most telomere-crisis cells die. The thick branch is the majority. The thin branch is the cancer. One geometric change, and the biology reads itself.
